name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
label: Jemaa el-Fnaa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier' (node/660578096): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1132585098: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jemaa El-Fna' (528 m across).
notes: The famous main square of the medina, lively at sunset.

text.description: Jemaa el-Fnaa is the main square of Marrakech. It sits in the medina, the old city, and is used by locals and visitors alike. It photographs well because there is always something going on: stalls, juice sellers, musicians and performers by day, and food stalls lit up once it gets dark. The city was founded in 1070, and the square began as an open market space next to a fortress. For centuries it hosted festivals, parades and other public events. One explanation of its name points to a mosque begun by the Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur (ruled 1578-1603), which was never finished and fell into ruin. In 2008 the square was included in UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, which recognises its living traditions rather than its buildings. For a view from above, the rooftop terrace of Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier is a well-known elevated viewpoint, where you can see the square with the stalls and crowds below. A major renovation of the square began in May 2025, so the scene may look different from older photos. At street level, ask before photographing people. Photo-prop monkeys and snake charmers charge per shot.
text.geographic_location: In the medina (old city) of Marrakech, where it forms the main square of the old town.
text.directions_text: Head for the medina in the centre of Marrakech and ask for Jemaa el-Fnaa. If you want the elevated view as well, the Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier terrace is reached through the ground-floor café. Ask at the café, and check on the day which side of the square it is on. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a general view across the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the crowd and stalls in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single stalls, performers or lit-up food stands without having to push through the crowd or lean over a terrace edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier (rooftop terrace of the café, reached through the ground-floor café). A wide, elevated view across the whole square with the Koutoubia minaret behind it, showing the stalls and crowds below. For an elevated alternative, go up to the rooftop terrace of Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier, which gives a wide, raised view of the stalls and crowds below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. From the terrace, if the Koutoubia minaret is in view, place it on one of the upper grid lines, with the busy square filling the lower two-thirds. For a second angle, Café de France also looks directly over the action on the square and suits the busy evening scene. At street level you can take close scenes of performers and food stalls, but ask permission before photographing people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky or the minaret, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours are not washed out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on the rail or your body to keep the phone still. Live Photos can capture the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, and arrive early because the terrace fills up. The light fades and the food stalls light up, so you can take both daytime and evening shots from the same area.

text.access_note: The square itself is an open public space, but the terrace is a café terrace where you must buy a drink (usually mint tea) to go up, so check the official site or the café for opening times, and check whether renovation work is affecting the square, before you go.

name: Majorelle Garden
label: Majorelle Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin Majorelle' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Majorelle Garden'.
notes: Cobalt-blue villa among cacti and palms.

text.description:
Majorelle Garden is a one-hectare botanical and artist's garden in Marrakech, known for its bold cobalt blue. The French painter Jacques Majorelle began it in 1923 and worked on it for almost forty years. He used the deep blue, now called Majorelle Blue, extensively in the garden and its buildings. The Cubist villa was designed by the architect Paul Sinoir in the 1930s. In the 1980s Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé rescued the neglected garden and restored it. Today the villa houses the Berber Museum, and the garden is known for its cacti, fountains and birdlife. It attracts more than 700,000 visitors a year.

The classic photo is from the northern edge of the central lily pond, looking at the blue villa. Papyrus stems frame both sides, blue ceramic pots sit in the foreground, and the villa is reflected in the water. The reflection is clearest when the water is calm, which is usually only at opening time. Two good alternatives are the water basin with its lilies and the pavilion by Bill Willis behind the palms, and a head-on view of the villa's front with cacti in the foreground. Photography inside the museums is not allowed, so keep your phone for the grounds.
text.geographic_location: Majorelle Garden is in Marrakech, Morocco. It began in 1923 as a plot on the edge of a palm grove, and the Yves Saint Laurent Museum now stands nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The garden is called Jardin Majorelle. Once inside, follow the paths to the central lily pond. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the villa and its reflection, as it keeps the scene natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the lily basin and the pavilion, so the water and palms fit together. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the blue pots, cacti or a single papyrus frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stand at Jardin Majorelle, on the northern edge of the central lily pond, facing the blue villa across the water. From here you see the villa reflected in still water, with papyrus on both sides and blue ceramic pots in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the villa's base near the lower third, so the water takes up the bottom of the frame and the reflection mirrors the building. Hold the phone low, just above the pots, to make them a strong foreground. For a second shot, move to the basin to photograph the lilies and the Bill Willis pavilion, or to the cross-path just before the villa for a head-on view with cacti in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the villa to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the blue stays rich rather than washed out. Take a few frames in a row, as the reflection changes when the water ripples. Use portrait mode only for close-ups of pots or plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At opening (8am), before the water is disturbed and other visitors arrive. Opening hours vary by season, so check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden with timed entry, and tickets are sold online, so check the official site before you go. Photography inside the museums is not allowed.

name: La Mamounia
label: La Mamounia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardins de La Mamounia' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardins de La Mamounia' (way/126306407): middle (470 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3210501: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: La Mamounia is a five-star hotel opposite the Kutubiyya Mosque in Marrakech, and its gardens offer a quieter, greener view of it. From the garden you see open lawns and palm-lined paths, with the back of the hotel rising behind them. The result is a soft, green picture that is quite different from the hotel's grand interiors. The hotel was conceived in 1923 by architects Henri Prost and Antoine Marchisio and opened in 1929, mixing Moroccan architecture with Art Deco. It stands on a palace and garden that Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah gave to his son, Moulay Mamoun, in the 18th century. The garden still covers about 8.1 hectares, so there is room to walk around and try different angles. Look for long views down a palm-lined path, with the building closing the scene at the far end. If you also pass the outer courtyard and façade near the entrance, they make a good second picture, framed by palms and walkways. The famous marble corridor and the spa pool are inside the hotel and are not free public spots, so plan your photos around the gardens and the entrance area. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, and keep the phone level so the palm trunks stand straight. Because this is a hotel, check at the entrance on Avenue Bab Jdid whether you can walk into the gardens before you go.
text.geographic_location: La Mamounia is in central Marrakech, directly opposite the Kutubiyya Mosque. The gardens lie behind the hotel building. The hotel's entrance is on Avenue Bab Jdid; check there whether visitors can enter the gardens.
text.directions_text: Start from the Kutubiyya Mosque, which is directly opposite the hotel, and arrive on foot, or use any local transport of your choice. Go to the entrance on Avenue Bab Jdid and check there whether you can enter the gardens. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lawn, path and hotel in one picture. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the garden in the frame, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the building between the palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardins de La Mamounia (garden area behind the hotel building). Open lawns and palm-lined garden paths with the hotel's rear buildings in the background, a softer green alternative to the hotel's architecture. From here the hotel lies to the north-west, and you look across open lawns and palm-lined paths towards its rear buildings. If you would rather photograph the hotel from the front, the outer courtyard and façade near the entrance are a second option, framed by palms and walkways.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a garden path up with one of the vertical lines so it leads the eye towards the building. Keep a few palms in the foreground to add depth. Hold the phone level when using 0.5x, because tilting it will bend the building's edges. For a second picture, move to the entrance area and frame the façade between the palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building or the lawn to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the pale walls or sky look washed out. Portrait mode works well for close-ups of palm leaves or garden details, but keep normal photo mode for wide views.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the lawns and walls look warmer. At midday the palm shade and bright walls can make the contrast harsh.

text.access_note: The gardens belong to a hotel, so check at the entrance on Avenue Bab Jdid, and on the official site, before you go to see whether visitors may enter.

name: Menara Gardens
label: Menara Gardens
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1920259: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Olive-grove garden with a pavilion reflected in a pool and the Atlas behind.

text.description: The Menara Gardens are a large, flat public garden and olive orchard on the western side of Marrakech. At the centre is a big rectangular water basin, about 195 metres long and 160 metres wide, with a two-storey pavilion on its edge. That calm, open water gives you a simple, uncluttered picture: green trees, still water and a neat pavilion with plenty of sky above. The gardens were first laid out around 1157 under the Almohad ruler Abd al-Mu'min. The pavilion you see now was completed in 1870, on the ruins of an earlier Saadian one. The gardens are part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for Marrakech, and the view of the pavilion and basin with the High Atlas Mountains behind is often called an iconic image of the city. From the phone icon on the map you are close to the pavilion, so you can take in the scene without a long walk. Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky, and use 2x or 3x to pick out the pavilion's arches and balcony. Walk a little way along the basin to try different angles, and keep the phone level using the gridlines.
text.geographic_location: The Menara Gardens lie on the western side of Marrakech, outside the historic city walls and very close to Menara Airport. The Kutubiyya Mosque is to the north-east.
text.directions_text: No Marrakech tram or railway stop serves this spot, so the easiest way from the old city (the medina) is by taxi or hired scooter, heading west and asking for the Menara Gardens. Walk north-west from the phone icon on the map to reach it. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the basin and pavilion together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a low, water-level view with more sky, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the pavilion's arches and balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. From here the mountains are behind you, not in the frame. For the classic pavilion-and-mountains shot, look south from the far side of the basin.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the water's edge on a lower line, so the pavilion sits on the grid with the trees beside it. Keep the phone level so the long edge of the basin does not slope. If the water is calm, include a little reflection. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one of the pavilion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bright sky does not wash out. If the surface is still, try a Live Photo to catch any small ripples or birds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a clear day, ideally in the softer light of the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower and the sky is less harsh. A clear day gives the best chance of seeing the High Atlas in the distance.

text.access_note: The Menara Gardens are a public garden, but access rules and any entry charge can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bahia Palace
label: Bahia Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palais de la Bahia' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Palais Bahia' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2465115: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: 19th-century palace with painted ceilings and courtyards.

text.description:
The Bahia Palace is a 19th-century palace in the old part of Marrakech. It was begun in the 1860s by the grand vizier Si Musa, and his son Si Ba Ahmed enlarged it between 1894 and 1900. It has around 150 rooms around a string of courtyards and garden courts, and covers almost 2 hectares. It photographs well because everything is decorated: painted wooden ceilings, carved stucco and zellij tilework all sit close together, so even a simple shot has colour and pattern in it.

The view most people want is the Grand Courtyard (the Cour d'Honneur), dated to 1896–7. It measures 50 by 30 metres, is paved in Carrara marble, and is framed by colourful wooden galleries. Standing close to the central fountain, you get the marble and water in the foreground, then the carved galleries, with palm trees rising behind the building.

The name means "the Brilliant", reportedly after Ba Ahmed's favourite wife. The palace was originally built on one level, although an upper floor was added in some parts after 1908.

For the best pictures, go early. The courtyards fill up with tour groups from late morning, and one guide suggests the area gets busier by the minute after opening. Two other shots are worth a look: a framed view back through a carved, painted doorway toward the interior, and the coloured light from the stained-glass windows in the Petit Riad.
text.geographic_location: The Bahia Palace is in the old city of Marrakech, just north of the Mellah quarter. The Dar Si Said museum, built by Ba Ahmed's brother, lies a little further north.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so navigate to the Bahia Palace, just north of the Mellah. Inside, you enter through a horseshoe-arch doorway and follow a long garden path to the Small Riad. The Grand Courtyard lies east of the Small Courtyard, so keep heading east through the palace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the marble floor, fountain and galleries in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the painted ceilings and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Grand Courtyard (Cour d'Honneur), standing close to the central fountain). The marble-paved courtyard and fountain in the foreground, with the palace's carved galleries and palm trees rising behind the building. In the Grand Courtyard (Cour d'Honneur), close to the central fountain. From here the marble-paved courtyard and fountain fill the foreground, and the palace's carved galleries and palm trees rise behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the fountain low in the frame, with the galleries filling the middle and the palm trees at the top. Keep the gridlines level so the gallery columns stay upright. For a second shot, try a view back through a carved, painted doorway toward the interior, or the coloured light from the stained-glass windows in the Petit Riad.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the galleries or the marble to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if bright areas look washed out. If the courtyard is busy, take a few frames and pick the one with the fewest people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early, right at opening, before the tour groups arrive. One guide says mid-morning light is best here, but it gets noticeably busier by then.

text.access_note: The palace is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for current entry details and opening times.

name: El Badi Palace
label: El Badi Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'El Badi Palace' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3241554: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'El Badi Palace' (347 m across).
notes: Ruined Saadian palace with storks nesting on the walls.

text.description: El Badi Palace is a large ruined royal palace in the Kasbah district. Its name means roughly "the Incomparable". Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of the Saadian dynasty commissioned it in 1578, and it was built to receive guests and show off his wealth, with materials brought in from as far apart as Italy and Mali. After his death in 1603 it was neglected, and its marble and other fittings were stripped out and reused in buildings elsewhere in Morocco. What remains are tall earthen walls, sunken gardens and an open courtyard, which makes for strong, simple compositions. The best wide view is from the top of the eastern rampart, where you look across the orange trees and the courtyard. The Koutoubia minaret may be seen in the distance, but check on the day, as it depends on clear weather; the Atlas mountains may show beyond it on a clear day. Storks nest on the walls, so keep a respectful distance and never disturb them. A second option is to shoot from courtyard level, where the long pool and sunken orange gardens sit between the high walls. The pool is not always filled, and event structures or scaffolding sometimes block part of the courtyard. Drones are generally not permitted here.
text.geographic_location: El Badi Palace stands in the Kasbah district on the southern side of Marrakech, close to the Kasbah Mosque and the Saadian Tombs.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Kasbah district and ask for El Badi Palace, going by taxi or on foot. Once inside, find the way up onto the eastern rampart. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of gardens, courtyard and walls. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for storks on the walls and, if it is visible, for pulling in the Koutoubia minaret. The default lens (1x) suits the courtyard-level view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the wide view, head for the eastern rampart on the eastern side of the site, away from the icon, at the top of the walls you climb. From there the palace spreads out below you, with the orange gardens and courtyard in front, and the Koutoubia minaret may be visible in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line, so the gardens fill most of the frame. Include a stretch of wall in the corner for scale. For a stork shot, zoom in and wait for a bird to settle against clear sky. If you go back down, the long pool and orange trees between the tall walls make a good second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the walls to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the storks stay dark and sharp. Try a panorama along the rampart for the whole palace, holding the phone steady and moving slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun lights the walls and the storks show up as silhouettes.

text.access_note: El Badi Palace is a ticketed site and the rampart view needs an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go for prices and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines with the horizon on the upper third line is a sensible way to compose this wide view.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit the whole garden and courtyard into one frame from the rampart.
Rampart tops can be uneven or exposed, so watch your footing while taking photos.

name: Saadian Tombs
label: Saadian Tombs
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15662474: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saadian Tombs' (105 m across).

text.description: The Saadian Tombs are a royal burial ground tucked inside the old kasbah (citadel) district of Marrakech, just behind the Kasbah Mosque. Most of what you see dates from the Saadian dynasty, especially the reign of Ahmad al-Mansur (1578–1603). Many art historians regard the complex as the high point of Moroccan architecture of that period. It photographs well because the richly decorated rooms sit beside open garden space, so you can shoot both ornate interiors and calmer outdoor scenes. There are two main buildings. The older eastern mausoleum is flanked by gardens. The western one is next to today's visitor entrance and holds the Chamber of the Mihrab, the Chamber of the Twelve Columns and the Chamber of the Three Niches. Ahmad al-Mansur was buried in the centre of the Twelve Columns chamber in 1603, and other family members were laid there with him later. Start with a wide view of the garden and the outside of the buildings, then go in for the decoration. Rooms can be dim and space is limited, so move slowly, keep your phone steady against a wall or doorway, and step aside for other visitors. Look for repeating patterns, columns and the light falling on the walls. The phone icon on the map is at the heart of the complex, so most of your shots will be taken close to the subject.
text.geographic_location: The tombs are in Marrakech's royal kasbah (citadel) district, on the south side of the Kasbah Mosque.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is close to this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or hired scooter to the Kasbah district and the Kasbah Mosque. The tombs are on the south side of the mosque, and the visitor entrance is beside the western building. If you are already in the Kasbah area, walk round to the south of the mosque and follow the signs or ask a local. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the garden and the larger chambers, and the default lens (1x) for most general shots. Switch to telephoto (2x–5x, depending on your phone) for carved and painted details, columns and inscriptions that you cannot get close to.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the open garden space between the buildings, then move to doorways to look into the chambers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up walls and columns with them so the architecture looks straight. In the Chamber of the Twelve Columns, frame the columns so they lead towards the centre of the room. Add a doorway or arch in the foreground for depth. Use a telephoto shot for one detail, such as a pattern or an inscription panel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the decoration keeps its detail. In dim rooms, hold your phone steady against a wall or doorframe and let night mode work if it switches on by itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when it is quiet, ideally early or late in the day, to avoid crowds and harsh midday sun. Check the official site for visiting times.

text.access_note: This is a major visitor attraction and may be ticketed or have timed entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kutubiyya Mosque
label: Koutoubia Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Koutoubia Gardens' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Koutoubia Gardens' (way/435129470): middle (173 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12255861: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Koutoubia Mosque' (140 m across).
notes: The 12th-century minaret is the city's best-known landmark.

text.description: The Kutubiyya Mosque, also spelled Koutoubia, is the largest mosque in Marrakech, and its minaret is an important landmark and symbol of Marrakech. The tower is 77 metres tall and decorated with different geometric arch patterns, with a spire and metal orbs on top. The mosque was founded in 1147 and rebuilt around 1158, and the minaret was probably finished around 1195. The name means 'booksellers', after the book trade that once filled the streets around its base. It photographs well because the tower is tall, decorated with geometric arch patterns and sits above open gardens, so you can get the whole height in one frame. The gardens stretch along the south and west sides of the mosque, and palms, orange trees and roses frame the minaret. Fountains and pools can add foreground interest. As the light fades the stone turns gold or ochre, which is why sunset is a popular time. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims, so every photo is taken from outside. If you want a more architectural frame, the old stone archway and the ruins of the earlier prayer hall near the mosque give a different view, with arches around the minaret. One review mentions construction work there, so check when you arrive. Keep your phone upright and let the tower fill the height of the screen. Take a few shots from slightly different spots, as palms and branches can cover the top.
text.geographic_location: In the southwest medina quarter of Marrakech, on Avenue Mohammed V opposite Place de Foucauld, about 200 metres west of the Jemaa el-Fnaa market square. Large gardens lie on its west and south sides.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to start from. If you are coming from elsewhere in Marrakech, get to the Koutoubia Mosque by whatever local transport suits you, or walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa. The mosque is about 200 metres west of the square, which is about 3 minutes on foot. Then continue to the south side of the mosque, into Koutoubia Gardens. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole minaret with palms and trees around it. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, such as a pool or flower beds, and keep the tower in the middle so it doesn't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the decorated upper part and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Koutoubia Gardens (south and west sides of the gardens). The full height of the minaret framed by palms, orange trees and roses, with the stone turning gold or ochre as the light fades. From there the minaret is to the north. This is the classic free place to see the full height of the tower, framed by palms, orange trees and roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line. Hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the sides lean inwards. Put a palm or a fountain or pool in the foreground and leave a little sky above the spire. If you want a less crowded, more architectural view, the old archway and the ruins of the earlier prayer hall near the mosque also frame the minaret, if they are open when you visit.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone of the minaret to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the stone keeps its golden colour. At dusk, use night mode only if the scene is dark, and brace your elbows against your body to keep still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the minaret is lit golden. Sunset is the most popular choice, while sunrise is likely to have fewer people.

text.access_note: Koutoubia Gardens are a free open space, but the mosque itself is closed to non-Muslims and works nearby may affect some areas, so check on arrival.
claims_not_in_sources: From the gardens the default lens (1x) should fit most or all of the minaret, depending on exactly where you stand.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky detail and the golden colour of the stone at sunset.
Sunset tends to be busier than sunrise.

name: Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakesh
label: YSL Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Musée Yves Saint Laurent' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Musée Yves Saint Laurent' (way/672043449): middle (77 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q30727522: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Modern brick-patterned museum beside Majorelle Garden.

text.description: The Yves Saint Laurent Museum is a modern building in earthy tones, made of cubes and curves and covered in a lacework of bricks that recalls woven fabric. It is built from terracotta, concrete and terrazzo, and the bricks were made locally from Moroccan earth. That texture is what makes it photograph well: the pattern looks good in a wide shot and even better up close. The museum opened to the public on 19 October 2017 and covers 4,000 square metres. It was designed by Studio KO, and in 2018 it won Wallpaper magazine's award for best new public building. It stands on Yves Saint Laurent Street, close to Majorelle Garden. The most popular picture is the close frame of the entrance with the large YSL lettering and the façade behind it. Other visitors usually want the same shot, so there can be a queue. Take it early or near closing time if you can. For a calmer image, step back to the street for a head-on view of the latticed front, with people posing by the entrance. Le Studio Café offers a quieter view of the architecture from the courtyard, but you may need a ticket to get in. Photography rules inside the grounds can vary, so check on arrival.
text.geographic_location: In Marrakech, on Yves Saint Laurent Street, near Majorelle Garden.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. Search for 'Yves Saint Laurent Museum' or 'Majorelle Garden' in a map app, as the two are close together. Once you are on Yves Saint Laurent Street, the entrance with the large YSL lettering is easy to spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the entrance and logo. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole front of the building from the street. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for close-ups of the brick lattice.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the entrance with the YSL logo). A close frame of the museum's entrance and its large YSL lettering, with the building's façade behind. If the queue is long, the street (Rue Yves Saint Laurent) gives a head-on view of the terracotta front, and Le Studio Café gives a calmer view of the architecture from the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the lettering up with one of the lines so the logo sits clearly in the frame. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the brickwork stay straight. For a wider picture, step back and include the pattern of the façade and any visitors posing in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the logo or the brick wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the light-coloured lettering looks washed out. Use portrait mode only if you are photographing a person in front of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or near closing time, to avoid the queue at the logo.

text.access_note: Photo rules can change, so check on the day before visiting.

name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
label: Ben Youssef Madrasa
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1770461: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ben Youssef Madrasa' (83 m across).
notes: Former Islamic college with a stunning carved courtyard.

text.description:
The Ben Youssef Madrasa was a college for Islamic students, and it is one of the most important historical buildings in Marrakech. It was finished in 1564-65 under the Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib and takes its name from the neighbouring Ben Youssef Mosque. At its height it was the largest madrasa in the Maghreb, with 130 student rooms and space for up to 800 students. It closed in 1960, reopened as a historical site in 1982, and reopened again in April 2022 after a restoration that began in November 2018.

For a phone camera, the draw is the central courtyard. A shallow rectangular pool, roughly 3 by 7 metres, sits in the middle. Around it the walls are layered: zellij tilework low down, calligraphy at eye level, carved stucco above, and finally carved wooden eaves. Because everything is arranged symmetrically, a straight-on shot looks balanced almost without effort. The pool can add a soft reflection of the arches.

The building is almost square, about 40 by 43 metres. That means you are always fairly close to the walls, so the wide view and the close-up detail are both easy to get. Look for the muqarnas (honeycomb-like) vault at the entrance, the bronze-plated doors, and the carved cedar lintel above them. Move slowly and let other visitors pass through the frame before you press the shutter. Check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In Marrakech, right next to the Ben Youssef Mosque, which gave the madrasa its name.
text.directions_text: No Underground, metro or tram stops are near this spot, so start from the Ben Youssef Mosque, because the madrasa is next to it. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the building itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard, where space is tight, so you can fit the pool and the surrounding galleries into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for calmer, less stretched views of the arches. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as carved stucco, tilework and the entrance vault.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at the edge of the courtyard near the pool, facing along its length, so the galleries run symmetrically on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the pool up with the middle of the frame so the symmetry shows. Crouch low and hold the phone close to the water for a reflection. For detail shots, pick one band of the wall, such as tiles, calligraphy or carved wood, and fill the frame with it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the walls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky above the courtyard does not wash out the carving. Portrait mode works for a person standing in an archway, but keep them a little way from the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter for clear shots of the courtyard. When the sun is higher, light reaches further into the courtyard, though the contrast between sunlit and shaded walls can be strong.

text.access_note: The madrasa is a historical site that people visit; check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.

name: Ben Youssef Mosque
label: Ben Youssef Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ben Youssef Madrasa' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Medersa Ben Youssef' (relation/1770461): middle (83 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1770462: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ben Youssef Mosque' (96 m across).
notes: Historic medina mosque near the madrasa.

text.description: The Ben Youssef Mosque is one of the most important mosques in Marrakech. It is named after the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf, who built a grand central mosque in this area, completed between 1120 and 1132. The building you see today is a rebuild finished in 1819-20, with a minaret of around 40 metres. From the street it is hard to photograph, because high walls hide most of it. The best-known photograph in this area is taken next door, in the central courtyard of the Ben Youssef Madrasa. This former theological college was founded in 1563-64, just east of the mosque. Photo guides often call this the postcard view of the complex. It works well on a phone because the symmetry is simple: pool in the foreground, arches behind, sky above. The courtyard belongs to the madrasa, not the mosque, so the mosque itself is not in the frame. For the mosque and its minaret, look along the lanes nearby. Rue Azbezt is a recommended place for a view of the minaret and the complex rising at the end of the lane. Be discreet around worshippers and other visitors, and ask before photographing people.
text.geographic_location: In the Medina quarter of Marrakech. The mosque sits beside the Ben Youssef Madrasa, which lies just to its east, and the Almoravid Qubba is nearby.
text.directions_text: Head for the Ben Youssef Madrasa in the Medina quarter. From there the mosque is about 95 m to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the courtyard view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the arches are cut off at the sides, and keep the phone level so the lines do not lean. Telephoto (2x-5x) suits carved details and the minaret when you can see it between the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Ben Youssef Madrasa (central courtyard, standing across the reflecting pool and facing the arches). The tiled courtyard with its still pool reflecting the arches and galleries, a composition often called the postcard view of the complex. On the far side of the reflecting pool from the arches, and face the arches. The pool should fill the lower part of your frame, with the galleries behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the pool's edge on a lower line, with the arches centred. Crouch and hold the phone low to catch more reflection. For the mosque side, try the lane called Rue Azbezt, where the minaret and complex rise at the end, or the arched entrance with its carved doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiles or arches to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright stonework keeps its detail. Take a second shot a moment later in case ripples spoil the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Right at opening, when the pool is calm and the courtyard is empty.

text.access_note: The mosque itself is not open to non-Muslim visitors, and the madrasa courtyard is a ticketed site, so check current ticket details before you go; one guide notes that entry is cash only.

name: Marrakech Museum
label: Marrakech Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4627685: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Marrakech Museum' (95 m across).
notes: Palace with a grand central courtyard and chandelier.

text.description: The Marrakech Museum is set inside the Dar Mnebhi Palace, a palace built at the start of the 20th century by Mehdi al-Mnebhi, a minister of war under Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz. It later became a girls' school, and was carefully restored and opened as a museum in 1997. The photograph to take here is the central courtyard. It is now paved and roofed over, and it is surrounded by galleries with colourful zellij tilework and painted, carved cedar wood. Fountains sit in the middle of the space, and a very large brass chandelier, cut into geometric and arabesque patterns, hangs above them. The pattern, colour and symmetry make it an easy place to take strong phone photos, and the covered courtyard keeps the light soft and even. Look up as well as across: the chandelier is the centrepiece, and the carved wood and galleries give you plenty of layers to work with. The palace also has a hammam with domed and vaulted chambers, and the collection includes carpets, costumes, pottery and Berber jewellery, which can make simple close-up pictures. Interiors can be dim, so hold your phone steady and keep your arms close to your body. Rules on photography inside, and on entry, can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the old centre of Marrakech, inside the former Dar Mnebhi Palace.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the old centre of Marrakech and head for the Marrakech Museum, or take a taxi or hired scooter to the area. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so once you are at the building you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole courtyard, then switch to the default lens (1x) for calmer, less stretched views of the fountains and galleries. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the tilework or the chandelier.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, the courtyard and its fountains are your main subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the chandelier with the centre of the courtyard for a symmetrical shot. Then step to one side and include a gallery arch or a tiled wall as a foreground frame. Keep your phone level so the straight lines of the galleries do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the brightest part of the courtyard, then lower the exposure slider a little so the chandelier and lit areas keep their detail. If the interior is dim, use night mode and hold still for a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the museum is open and less busy, so you can get clear shots of the courtyard without many people in the frame. Because the courtyard is roofed over, the time of day matters less than it would outdoors.

text.access_note: This is a museum housed in a historic palace, so access is likely to be ticketed and have set hours: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The covered courtyard gives soft, even light, so the time of day matters less than outdoors.
Interiors can be dim, so night mode may help.
The museum can be busier at some times of day than others, and visiting when it is quieter helps with clear shots.
Rules about photography and entry inside the museum can change.
Access is likely ticketed with set opening hours.

name: Bab Agnaou
label: Bab Agnaou
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue de la Kasbah' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rue de la Kasbah nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/374299688: the OpenStreetMap point 'باب أكناو'.

text.description: Bab Agnaou is one of the best-known gates in Marrakech and was the main public entrance to the royal Kasbah, the citadel in the southern medina. Its construction is attributed to the Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur, and it was finished around 1188 or 1190. It photographs well because of the carving. Around the original arch are alternating semi-circular bands, some with radiating lines and some with interlacing arches. The corners are filled with floral patterns, each with a small carved shell, and a long band of Quranic lettering frames the whole façade. The stone is sandstone, so it takes on a warm colour in low sun. The gate has changed over the centuries. The flanking towers have gone, and the arch was later partly filled in with a smaller, plainer brick arch. That is why the carved frame looks bigger than the opening beneath it. The gate stands on a busy road, so traffic and people walking through can spoil a straight-on shot. Take your time, wait for a gap, and keep your phone steady as you shoot. For a quieter picture with more detail in the carving, try the Kasbah side of the gate on Rue de la Kasbah. If you want the full arch with its bands framed straight-on, the open space outside the gate is the alternative.
text.geographic_location: Bab Agnaou is in the southern part of the Marrakech medina, at the north-western corner of the Kasbah, close to Bab er-Robb. The Kasbah is the royal quarter that also holds the Kasbah Mosque, the El Badi Palace and the Saadian Tombs.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby train, metro or tram stops for this spot. Head for the Kasbah in the southern medina and use a map app to navigate to Bab Agnaou. Take care near the road, as traffic passes close to the gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the gate and the street behind it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the carved bands and the lettering without walking into the traffic. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is quiet and you want the whole setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue de la Kasbah (Kasbah side, inside the gate looking back toward the carved façade). A closer, less crowded view of the gate's carved decoration, with the Kasbah streets leading away behind it. From here you get a closer, less crowded view of the decoration, with the Kasbah streets leading away behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the arch with the middle of the frame so the symmetry reads clearly. Let the Kasbah street lead the eye towards the gate. If you want the full arch with its concentric carved bands framed straight-on, the open space outside the gate is a good second spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the carved stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sandstone does not turn pale and lose its detail. Hold the phone with both hands and take a few frames, so you can choose one without a passer-by in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour gives warm light on the stone. Midday is the busiest and hardest time to shoot, with heavy crowds and traffic.

text.access_note: The gate is a working city gate on a public road, and no ticket is needed for viewing it; check locally before you go if you plan anything beyond looking from the street.

name: Bab Doukkala
label: Bab Doukkala
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bab Doukkala Mosque' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12195551: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic gate on the western medina wall.

text.description:
Bab Doukkala is the main north-western gate of Marrakech's old walled city, and the phone icon on the map sits at the gate itself, with the Bab Doukkala Mosque right beside it. That makes it a good place for a quieter second picture once you have photographed the gate. The mosque is a Saadian-era building, and its entrance and minaret are the subject here. The minaret gives you a strong vertical line against the sky, and the doorway gives a more intimate, human-scale frame.

The gate is much older than the mosque. It dates back to around 1126, when the Almoravid emir Ali ibn Yusuf built the city's first walls. It has kept its original bent entrance: the passage turns at a right angle twice, so you enter from the west, turn south, then turn east before coming out into the city. Simple extra openings on either side now let people and traffic move through more easily.

For the gate, step back into the street in front of it so the large horseshoe-shaped arch and its two flanking towers fit in the frame. The open square in front also lets you include the gate and the historical marker together. The area is busy, with the city's main intercity bus terminal just outside and slightly north of the gate, so expect traffic and people passing through your shot. Take your time, and keep an eye on the roads when you cross.
text.geographic_location: Bab Doukkala is on the north-western edge of the Marrakech medina, where the old walls meet the busy roads outside. The mosque stands right next to the gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the north-western side of the medina and ask for Bab Doukkala. The city's main intercity bus terminal is just outside and slightly north of the gate, which makes a useful landmark. The phone icon on the map is at the gate itself, so you will not need to walk any further once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the mosque entrance. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x) for the minaret and its details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole gate and the square in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, turn to the neighbouring mosque and photograph its entrance and minaret, a quieter subject next to the gate. Photograph the mosque from outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the minaret on one vertical line so it does not lean. Include a little of the doorway at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. For another view, walk a short way out into the square, where you can fit the gate's horseshoe arch, its two towers and the historical marker into one picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the minaret or the doorway to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its colour. If you use 0.5x, keep the phone level to avoid stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon tends to give softer light and fewer people and vehicles around the bus area.

text.access_note: The gate and square are open public space, but the mosque is a place of worship, so photograph it from outside and be discreet around people at prayer; check locally before you go.

name: Dar Si Said
label: Dar Si Said
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3329122: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Dar Si Said is a late 19th-century palace in Marrakech, built between 1894 and 1900 for Si Sa'id ibn Musa, a vizier and minister of defence. Today it is the National Museum of Weaving and Carpets. It photographs well because it is full of the ornament people come to Marrakech to see: carved and painted wood, patterned surfaces and a large riad garden with a central pavilion of painted wood. Unlike the nearby Bahia Palace, it is built over more than one level, so you get a sense of height and layers as well as the courtyard. There is also a grand reception hall on the upper floor.

The museum reopened in 2018 after renovation, with its displays now focused on weaving and Moroccan carpets. It was badly damaged in the September 2023 earthquake and closed for repairs, so how much you can see inside may vary. Check the official site before you go.

For your phone, treat the building as a set of small scenes rather than one big view. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in a whole space, then move closer for carved details and patterns. Keep your gridlines on so doorways and pavilion edges stay straight, and tap on the brightest part of the scene, then lower the exposure slider slightly to keep the colours rich.
text.geographic_location: Dar Si Said is in Marrakech, Morocco, north of the Bahia Palace, which was built further south.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops for this spot. Use the map to reach the phone icon on the map. If you start from the Bahia Palace, walk north to reach Dar Si Said. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and garden pavilion. Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) in tight rooms or the courtyard. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved wood, painted ceilings and tile patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It sits right at the palace, so the subject is directly around you. From here, frame the building and its garden side on, and keep the rest of the scene for after you have your main shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up doorways, columns and the garden pavilion with the vertical lines. Include a doorway or archway in the foreground to frame the scene. If the museum is open, take one wide shot of each room, then a close shot of a single detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so painted and carved surfaces keep their colour. If you are indoors in dim light, hold still and let night mode work, or brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the museum is open and quiet. Soft daylight in the morning usually suits courtyards and gardens, with fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a museum that was closed for repairs after the September 2023 earthquake, so check the official site before you go for current access.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning daylight usually suits courtyards and gardens.
Museums and courtyards are often quieter earlier in the day.
Interior rooms may be dim, which is when night mode helps.

name: Almoravid Qubba
label: Almoravid Qubba
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Almoravid Koubba' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/614070192: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Almoravid Qubba' (13 m across).

text.description:
The Almoravid Qubba is a small domed pavilion from the early 12th century. It was built under the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf and is the only surviving example of Almoravid architecture in Marrakech. Scholars think it was an ablutions pavilion for the nearby Ben Youssef Mosque, a place to wash before prayer. The building is only 12 metres tall and sits next to the Marrakech Museum. It is a quick stop, but it gives you a very different shape from the larger palaces and gates in the medina.

It photographs well because the dome and upper body stand out clearly as a single, compact subject. Inside, the carving is richly detailed, with floral patterns, calligraphy and some of the earliest muqarnas (honeycomb-style vaulting) in Morocco. Over half of the building was buried under 7-8 metres of debris until French scholars excavated it from the late 1940s, so it now sits below street level.

For a phone photo, the street-side view is the easy one. Stand on the pavement outside the fence and frame the dome and upper body through the railings. Get close to the fence, tap on the stonework so the bars stay soft, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. If you want a wider scene, a view may be possible from the square in front of the enclosure; check the exact spot on the map.
text.geographic_location: In the medina of Marrakech, right next to the Marrakech Museum and about 40 metres south of the Mosque of Ben Youssef.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is given for this spot, so head into the medina towards the Mosque of Ben Youssef. The Qubba is about 40 metres south of it, about 1 minute on foot. Walk the last stretch and look for the Marrakech Museum, which is right beside it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the dome through the railings. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step back and want the whole pavilion and its surroundings. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and upper details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Shoot from the pavement just outside the fence, nearest that point. From there the photo shows the dome and upper body of the small pavilion, framed through the railings. If you want more context, a wider view may be possible from the square in front of the enclosure, so check on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone close to the railings and tap the dome to focus, so the bars blur out. Turn on gridlines and line up the walls with the vertical lines so they don't lean. Try one wide shot that includes the fence and the sunken setting, then a closer one of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case a passer-by walks into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft and the pavement is quieter, such as early morning or late afternoon. Midday sun can leave the sunken enclosure in hard shadow.

text.access_note: The street-side view is from the pavement, but going inside the enclosure to see the interior may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mouassine Fountain
label: Mouassine Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mouassine Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q58974467: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic fountain in the Mouassine quarter.

text.description:
The Mouassine Fountain is a carved cedar-and-marble drinking fountain on a street in the medina of Marrakech. It belongs to the Mouassine Mosque complex, built between 1562-63 and 1572-73 on the orders of the Saadian sultan Abdallah Al-Ghalib. It is one of the largest fountains in the medina. The main arch has a projecting canopy of carved, painted wood, and beside it are three more arches that once led to troughs. The large fountain was for people, and the troughs were for watering animals, especially donkeys. Together the four arches fill a space about 18 metres long and 4.7 metres wide.

It photographs well because the detail is rich but close at hand: painted floral patterns on the wood, a carved plaster frieze with an eight-pointed star, and the basin below. It is also easy to walk past, so look for the carved wooden awning. The best frame is a straight-on view of the basin and its canopy, with the three arches running along beside it. Take a few steps back to get the whole width in, then move in for the carving. The painted colours are faded in places, so the texture of the wood and plaster often makes a better picture than the colour. A visitor has reported renovation work here, so part of the view may be covered. If so, shoot what you can see and try the street-level alternative along Rue El Mouassine.
text.geographic_location: In the medina of Marrakech, on the street edge of the Mouassine Mosque complex, at the northern side of the mosque's ablutions room. It sits in the Mouassine quarter, among the everyday streets of the quarter.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head into the Marrakech medina on foot and look for the Mouassine Mosque complex in the Mouassine quarter. The fountain is on the street side, with its carved wooden awning and three arches. Once you are at the phone icon on the map, the fountain is right in front of you. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the basin and its carved awning. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit all four arches in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close shots of the carved and painted wood.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the carved marble basin under the painted wooden awning, with the arched troughs alongside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the arch and the vertical posts so the facade does not lean. Place the basin low in the frame and the carved awning above it. Then take a wider shot along the three arches. As an alternative, step into Rue El Mouassine for a shot of the fountain facade with the street life of the quarter behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the carved woodwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky or street makes the shaded awning look washed out. Take a Live Photo if people are passing, so you can pick the moment when the frame is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the quarter is quieter and less crowded.

text.access_note: The fountain is a free, open-air street feature, but the mosque complex beside it is a place of worship, so be respectful and check locally before you go.
